Treat each `Iff` as an equivalence between two independently valid general facts; there is no need to derive either side from the other.

For the first `Iff`, use the representation of convolution as the pushforward of the product measure under multiplication. Tonelli’s theorem, with the `SFinite ν` assumption, gives
\[
\int f\,d(\mu * \nu)=\int_M\!\int_M f(xy)\,d\nu(y)\,d\mu(x).
\]
For absolute continuity, test a \(\rho\)-null set \(A\). Left invariance makes each section
\[
\{y:xy\in A\}
\]
\(\rho\)-null; then \(\nu\ll\rho\) makes it \(\nu\)-null. The convolution formula for sets, or the preceding integral identity applied to \(1_A\), therefore shows \((\mu*\nu)(A)=0\).

For the second `Iff`, work directly with values on a \(\nu\)-null set \(A\). If every \(\mu_i\ll\nu\), then every \(\mu_i(A)=0\), so
\[
\Bigl(\sum_i\mu_i\Bigr)(A)=\sum_i\mu_i(A)=0.
\]
Likewise,
\[
(\mu_1+\mu_2)(A)=\mu_1(A)+\mu_2(A),
\]
and a sum in `ENNReal` is zero exactly when both summands are zero. This proves both directions of the binary-addition characterization.

Thus the Lean proof can establish these four standard facts—preferably via the existing convolution-integral and absolute-continuity lemmas—and assemble the two `Iff`s and outer `And`. The essential analytic assumption is `SFinite ν`, which supplies the Tonelli/Fubini step for convolution.
